title: Three vehicles, one path
hookLine: Tibetans describe practicing all three vehicles together: renunciation, compassion, and the diamond path

cards: A Tibetan monk gets dressed in the morning. The robes he puts on carry the vows of a monk: no killing, no stealing, a simple life. Before breakfast he recites a prayer to wake up for the sake of every living being.
Later, in the shrine room, he picks up the vajra and the bell and chants a mantra. Three things in one morning, and to him they aren't three separate religions or even three separate schools.
They're three layers of one practice, stacked like the floors of a house. Today: three vehicles, one path.

teach.b: First, the word vehicle. In Sanskrit it's yana, something that carries you. Buddhist texts speak of more than one vehicle toward awakening.
Tibetan teachers describe three, and their point is that one person can ride all three at once.

The first vehicle, as Tibetans frame it, is about seeing clearly that grasping brings suffering, and turning away from it: ethics, simplicity, the vows of personal liberation, the four thoughts that turn the mind from year one.

A word of care: this layer has sometimes been given a name that sounds like lesser, and Theravada Buddhists, who follow the way of the elders, describe their own path in their own terms and don't use that name for themselves.
In the Tibetan scheme, the first vehicle names a layer inside every practitioner, not someone else's school.
Third, the great vehicle: compassion. On top of renunciation sits bodhicitta, the wish to wake up not for yourself alone but for all beings, and the wisdom that sees things as empty of a fixed self.
Tonglen and mind training live here.

teach.h: THE DIAMOND PATH, ON TOP OF BOTH.

teach.b: On top of both sit the methods of tantra: mantra, visualization, the bond with a teacher. Tibetan teachers say this top floor stands on the lower ones, and without them it falls.
That's why a monk can keep the vows of a monk, the vows of a bodhisattva and the commitments of tantra all at the same time.

how: Tibetan Buddhists describe practicing three vehicles together, renunciation and ethics, the compassion of the bodhisattva, and the methods of tantra, and monastics may keep the vows of all three at once.

o: renunciation, compassion and the diamond path, as one
three separate Buddhist schools, and you must pick one
the three lifetimes it takes before anyone can wake up

s: in Tibetan teaching, you pick one vehicle and drop the others
Tibetan teachers describe practicing all three together, as layers.
the diamond vehicle stands on the lower two
Tibetan teachers say without renunciation and compassion it falls.
Theravada Buddhists call their own path by the Tibetan name for the first vehicle
they describe their own path in their own terms, as the way of the elders.

games.q: a Tibetan monk has taken a monk's vows, a bodhisattva's vows and the commitments of tantra. which does he keep today?
o: only the highest, the tantric ones.
games.why: in the Tibetan telling they're layers of one path, so a monk keeps all three at the same time.

practice: Take the three one at a time, a breath for each. Renunciation: loosen your grip a little on one thing you hold too tightly. Compassion: wish one person well.
The diamond path: let a mantra, if you have one, or a quiet hum rest in your chest; then hold all three together, as one breath.

wordCard.voice: Three vehicles. In Tibetan teaching, renunciation, compassion and the diamond path, practiced together as layers of one path, each standing on the one below. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: yana, a vehicle, something that carries you. it's the yana in Mahayana and Vajrayana.

carryVoice: Your line: all three at once. Three floors, one house. Same time tomorrow.

sources.ref: Tibetan teaching on the three vehicles and the three sets of vows
